trig-basic-identities-reciprocal-identit.title: Reciprocal identities
trig-basic-identities-reciprocal-identit.summary: Use reciprocal relationships of the six trigonometric functions while retaining their domains.

blocks.text: Reciprocal pairs are sine/cosecant, cosine/secant, and tangent/cotangent. A reciprocal is defined only if the original function value is nonzero. At an angle where the denominator vanishes, the reciprocal expression is undefined.

blocks.description: The last reciprocal form for cotangent requires tanθ to be defined and nonzero; the equivalent cotθ = cosθ/sinθ is defined whenever sinθ ≠ 0, including when cosθ = 0.

blocks.text: Study method: identify the original domain before transforming the expression.

blocks.title: Recover a reciprocal from sine
blocks.strategy: The sine value is nonzero, so its reciprocal exists.

blocks.title: Simplify a reciprocal product
blocks.problem: Simplify cosθ secθ on its original domain.
steps: Cancel the common nonzero factor to obtain 1.
blocks.check: At θ = π/2, the original expression remains undefined even though 1 is defined.

blocks.text: Do not confuse csc, sec, or cot with arcsin, arccos, or arctan. Do not extend an identity beyond its original domain. For example, cot(π/2)=0 even though 1/tan(π/2) is undefined.
Reference guide: Schaum’s Outline 4th ed., Chs. 2 and 8; Lial 10th ed., §§1.4, 5.1; Kelley, Ch. 7.

trig-basic-identities-quotient-identitie.title: Quotient identities
trig-basic-identities-quotient-identitie.summary: Convert tangent and cotangent to sine/cosine quotients and identify where each is defined.

blocks.text: Tangent is sine divided by cosine and cotangent is cosine divided by sine. Expressing both functions through sine and cosine often makes algebraic simplification easier.

blocks.description: At a point with cosθ=0, tangent is undefined but cotangent is zero. At a point with sinθ=0, cotangent is undefined but tangent is zero.

blocks.text: Study method: identify the original domain before transforming the expression.

blocks.title: Evaluate a quotient identity
blocks.problem: If sinθ=3/5 and cosθ=−4/5, find tanθ.
blocks.strategy: Since cosine is nonzero, divide sine by cosine.
blocks.check: Quadrant II has positive sine and negative tangent.

blocks.title: Simplify while keeping the domain
blocks.check: The equality holds only where cosθ ≠ 0; it is not a globally defined identity.

blocks.text: Never cancel cosθ across a denominator without retaining cosθ ≠ 0. In particular, tanθ·cotθ = 1 is valid only where both are defined.

blocks.explanation: cotθ = cosθ/sinθ would divide by zero.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial 10th ed., §§1.4, 5.1; Schaum’s Outline 4th ed., Ch. 8; Young 3rd ed., chapter on trigonometric identities.

trig-basic-identities-evenodd-and-cofunc.title: Even–odd and cofunction identities
trig-basic-identities-evenodd-and-cofunc.summary: Apply parity and cofunction relations to rewrite negative and complementary angles.

blocks.text: Sine and tangent are odd functions; cosine is even. Their reciprocals have matching parity (cosecant and cotangent odd; secant even). Cofunction identities interchange sine/cosine, tangent/cotangent, and secant/cosecant at complementary arguments.

blocks.description: These equations hold wherever both sides are defined; for example, the tangent/cotangent cofunction pair excludes sinθ = 0.

blocks.text: Study method: identify the original domain before transforming the expression.

blocks.title: Use an odd-function identity
blocks.strategy: Sine changes sign when the argument is negated.
blocks.check: The negative angle points into quadrant IV, where sine is negative.

blocks.title: Use a cofunction identity
blocks.strategy: Replace cosine of a complement with sine.

blocks.text: Do not assume every function is odd: cos(−θ)=cosθ, not −cosθ. A complement is π/2−θ (or 90°−θ), not π−θ.

blocks.explanation: Secant is even wherever cosθ is nonzero.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial 10th ed., §§2.1, 5.1; Schaum’s Outline 4th ed., Chs. 3 and 6; Kelley, Ch. 7; Young, right-triangle and identity chapters.

trig-basic-identities-simplifying-trig-e.title: Simplifying trig expressions
trig-basic-identities-simplifying-trig-e.summary: Simplify mixed trigonometric expressions by selecting useful identities and preserving excluded angles.

blocks.text: Trigonometric simplification expresses an equivalent form on the same domain. Begin by identifying undefined denominators, then apply reciprocal, quotient, or Pythagorean identities. Factoring and common denominators can help.

blocks.description: The simpler result may be defined at extra angles. Always state the original-domain restriction in an equation of simplification.

blocks.text: Study method: identify the original domain before transforming the expression.

blocks.title: Reduce a ratio of trig functions
blocks.strategy: The original secant and tangent require cosθ≠0.
steps: Multiply by cosθ to get sinθ.
blocks.check: For θ=π/2, sinθ exists but the original quotient does not.

blocks.title: Factor using the Pythagorean identity
steps: Cancel one nonzero sine factor to get sinθ.
blocks.check: At θ=0, the original is 0/0, so the simplified answer does not add θ=0 to the domain.

blocks.text: Common mistakes: treating secθ as 1/sinθ, canceling across addition, or dropping angles where the original denominator vanishes.

blocks.explanation: 1−sin²θ=cos²θ; dividing by nonzero cosθ gives cosθ.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Schaum’s Outline 4th ed., Ch. 8; Lial 10th ed., §§5.1–5.2; Kelley, Ch. 7; Young, identities chapter.

trig-basic-identities-verifying-identiti.title: Verifying identities and domain restrictions
trig-basic-identities-verifying-identiti.summary: Prove trig identities on shared domains and distinguish algebraic proof from a numerical spot check.

blocks.text: A trigonometric identity is an equality for every angle in its stated common domain. Verification usually starts with one side, applies known identities or algebra, and reaches the other side. A few matching numerical values do not prove an identity.

blocks.description: The second statement has a common domain sinθ≠0; both sides are then defined. Verify algebraically by multiplying the numerator and denominator by 1+cosθ.

blocks.text: Study method: identify the original domain before transforming the expression.

blocks.title: Prove an identity by factoring
blocks.check: Both sides are defined for every real θ; the proof covers all real angles.

blocks.title: Prove a fractional identity safely
blocks.problem: Show (1−cosθ)/sinθ = sinθ/(1+cosθ) on the common domain.
steps: Multiply left numerator and denominator by (1+cosθ).
The numerator is 1−cos²θ=sin²θ, so the fraction becomes sin²θ/[sinθ(1+cosθ)] = sinθ/(1+cosθ).
blocks.check: θ=0 is excluded because the original left denominator is zero; θ=π is likewise excluded.

blocks.text: Do not divide by a trig factor before checking whether it can be zero. Never call a statement proved merely because it works at a single angle.

blocks.prompt: Is sin²θ+cos²θ=1 true at every real angle?
blocks.explanation: This identity follows from the unit circle and both sine and cosine are defined for all real θ.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial 10th ed., §5.2; Schaum’s Outline 4th ed., Ch. 8; Kelley, Ch. 7; Sullivan 9th ed., §3.4.
